Close the light-theme fork

The dark theme stays true black. This round decides the light half of “follow the OS.” Every preview places a native Compose capture from the unfolded Pixel 9 Pro Fold emulator inside its measured frame. The candidates use official Material 3 components, dynamic role mappings, type, targets and expanded-layout geometry audited against the supplied 2026-09-03 Google archive. Every selected state has a non-color cue, including a separate MD1-style 2dp tab indicator beneath the whole selected folder target rather than underlined link-like text. Open any preview to inspect the screen content at the cited dimensions.

Grilling round 1

Q1: What should separate surfaces in light mode?

The unfolded Pixel 9 Pro Fold is rendered at 852×883dp with the settled picker and transport on the left, Material’s centered 24dp expanded-layout spacer, and tracks on the right. Picker, transport and track section surfaces meet their screen edges without an extra rounded wrapper. The selectable letter rail is flush with the physical start edge; Open shares the Folders app-bar line; other controls respect system safety insets. App bars, buttons, lists, icons, slider, type and target geometry stay identical; only the Material surface-role hierarchy and decorative dividers change.

Pros
  • Uses MD3’s intended tonal hierarchy.
  • Looks calm and keeps attention on content.
  • Uses one separation mechanism.
Cons
  • Picker, transport and track surfaces are close in value.
  • Separation may weaken on poor panels or at low brightness.

My readSecond choice. Quiet and readable, but less immediate than 1c.

Pros
  • Separation stays explicit across panels and brightness levels.
  • Most directly mirrors dark mode’s structure.
Cons
  • Dividers at the pane, rail and every row create grid noise.
  • Light mode feels more administrative than the other treatments.

My readThird choice. Robust, but it spends too much visual ink.

Pros
  • Creates the clearest hierarchy with little linework.
  • Keeps the track list quiet while separating picker and transport.
  • Uses the requested white divider only at the rail seam.
Cons
  • Mixes tonal separation with one decorative divider.
  • The dim window gives light mode a heavier surrounding field.

DecisionChosen with the rail-seam divider changed to white.

Ranking: 1c > 1a > 1b 1c beats 1a because its pane hierarchy survives at a glance. 1a beats 1b because its softer separation avoids adding a divider to every row and region.

Q2: How prominent should true-peak values be in light mode?

Each track-pane detail uses the measured 426×883dp physical right half of the unfolded display: 12dp of the centered spacer plus the 414dp detail pane. Its frame is a crop from the fold center to the outer right edge, not a fictitious narrow phone. Every Material list item keeps duration plus true peak. Native Android system bars remain in the crop, and the track surface continues to the screen edges without a redundant rounded wrapper. Only supporting-value position and emphasis change.

Pros
  • Uses one simple rule in both themes.
  • Keeps supporting text subordinate to track titles.
  • Leaves every true-peak value available.
Cons
  • Duration and true peak receive equal emphasis despite different jobs.
  • The values recede in the light comparison.

DecisionChosen. Planned display templating lets users opt into stronger emphasis without hard-coding it into the default.

Pros
  • Makes true-peak values easy to scan across the folder.
  • Preserves every value without adding a column.
  • The weight difference is visible without competing with titles.
Cons
  • Introduces two treatments within one supporting line.
  • Repeated bold values add some visual texture.

My readFirst choice. Scannable without structural cost.

Pros
  • Makes every true-peak value vertically scannable.
  • Uses the Material list’s intended trailing-text slot.
  • Keeps all computed values available.
Cons
  • Reduces the width available to long track titles.
  • Reads more like the previously rejected table treatment.

My readThird choice. Very scannable, but too table-like for this list.

Ranking: 3b > 3a > 3c 3b beats 3a because it makes true peak scannable without structural cost. 3a beats 3c because keeping both values together preserves more width for track titles.
